claims.text: Dynamic evolution and stability of grain-boundary precipitates govern high-temperature plastic strain and toughness in tungsten-based plasma-facing materials.
Stabilized carbide or nitride precipitates along grain boundaries limit dislocation climb.
Stabilized carbide or nitride precipitates along grain boundaries limit grain-boundary sliding.
Limiting dislocation climb and grain-boundary sliding reduces high-temperature plastic deformation.
Engineering stable grain-boundary carbide or nitride precipitates enhances resistance to crack propagation.
A heat-treatment or alloying process can promote a controlled and stable distribution of carbide or nitride precipitates along tungsten-alloy grain boundaries.
Temperatures above 1000°C are representative of fusion plasma-facing service conditions for the proposed tungsten materials.
At elevated temperatures, plastic deformation in tungsten can occur through dislocation climb.
At elevated temperatures, plastic deformation in tungsten can occur through grain-boundary sliding.
Reinforcing tungsten grain boundaries with stable precipitates hinders high-temperature deformation mechanisms.
Hindering these deformation mechanisms reduces plastic strain.
Stable grain-boundary precipitates improve toughness by limiting crack initiation and propagation.
Relative to the unperturbed control, engineered samples will exhibit lower plastic strain during high-temperature testing.
Relative to the unperturbed control, engineered samples will exhibit higher fracture toughness during high-temperature testing.
The improved mechanical performance will correlate with a stable, well-dispersed grain-boundary precipitate network.
The hypothesis is expected to apply above 1000°C under quasi-static or cyclic loading in inert atmospheres.
Applicability under significant neutron irradiation remains uncertain.
Applicability to drastically different alloy systems remains uncertain.
